summary:
Vesper is a lunar landing-site navigator that tells mission planners, educators and the public where to land on the Moon for a given date. For any point on the Moon and any hour of 2027, it shows where the Sun and the Earth sit against the real terrain horizon, computed from NASA Moon Trek LOLA elevation models and JPL Horizons ephemerides. It then scores every candidate point for solar power, direct-to-Earth communication and slope, and recommends the best sites with a clear verdict and its reasons.
The challenge asks for a fast, intuitive way to compare landing sites and dates. Today that means crossing several expert tools point by point. Vesper does it in seconds: pick a region, a landing date and a mission length, and a "what if the landing slips?" slider shows instantly how a delay changes power and communication windows and where the new best site is. At the lunar south pole this matters: one week of delay can turn a top site (score 56) into an unusable one (score 2). Our hourly sunlight results match NASA's official LOLA illumination map with a correlation of 0.93 over 3,086 points.
details:
Vesper is a web app that helps mission planners, educators and the public decide where to land on the Moon for a given date. It opens on a 3D Moon lit by the true Sun, with the Earth at its true position for the selected hour. Users choose a landing date, a mission length, a priority (balanced, power or communications) and a maximum slope, and the Landing Site Navigator recommends sites in the region in view, each marked as suitable, acceptable or not recommended. A "what if the landing slips?" slider, from 0 to 29 days, recomputes everything instantly, so a schedule change becomes a quick check instead of a new analysis. Clicking any point of the Moon, or typing its coordinates, returns the verdict and its reasons, the position of the Sun and the Earth, the time left before sunset and Earthset, the continuous windows with Sun, Earth or both, and the solar energy for a vertical versus a horizontal panel. Each site panel adds an aptitude heat map with the three best points, a sky dial with the real terrain horizon, hourly visibility bands, terrain relief, slope and rover traversability. The catalogue covers 22 sites: Apollo 11 to 17, Chang'e 4, 5 and 6, Chandrayaan-3, SLIM, IM-1, IM-2, Blue Ghost 1, six south-pole candidate regions and two north-pole regions.

Behind the interface, JPL Horizons provides the Sun direction and the Earth position in the Moon-fixed frame for every hour of 2027; keeping the Earth's position, not just its direction, preserves the parallax between distant sites. For each point we ray-cast a 360° terrain horizon over NASA Moon Trek LOLA elevation models up to 150 km away, with exact lunar curvature and no refraction, since the Moon has no atmosphere. The 30 m/px polar models are used beyond 60° of latitude and the global model, about 237 m/px, elsewhere; multi-gigabyte files are read in windows, so the whole pipeline runs on a laptop and offline. The Sun or the Earth counts as visible when the centre of its disk is above the terrain horizon for an observer 2 m above the ground. Each point receives a score from 0 to 100 that weighs the share of hours with Sun, with Earth, with both, and the longest continuous sunlight in the mission window, and it is marked not recommended if its slope exceeds the limit or its score falls below 30. Solar energy is computed for a sun-tracking vertical panel and for a horizontal one. Precomputed regions of 21 × 21 points, 1 km apart, feed the app, and a Python server answers any other coordinate in about one second.

We validated the results against NASA data. Our hourly sunlight percentages match the LOLA average-illumination map, the layer shown in LROC QuickMap, with a correlation of 0.93 over 3,086 points in seven south-pole regions, and regional averages differ by only 0 to 2.4 percentage points. Moon Trek elevations agree with the landing elevations published by the LROC team within 4 to 20 m at Chang'e 4, Chang'e 6, SLIM and IM-1, and the precomputed ephemeris agrees with direct Horizons queries within 0.001°.

The main benefit is speed when plans change. When hardware or launch delays move a landing date, planners can see in seconds whether a site still works and which nearby site is best, instead of crossing several expert tools point by point; at the Connecting ridge, one week of delay drops a top site from a score of 56 to 2. The same view explains to students and the public why the lunar poles are so demanding: the Sun skims the horizon, a horizontal solar panel there collects almost nothing (0 kWh/m² against 155 kWh/m² for a vertical one), and far-side sites never see the Earth and need relay satellites. We hope Vesper becomes a shared decision aid for science and engineering teams choosing landing sites and dates, and an intuitive way to teach lunar lighting. Next steps include more years of ephemeris, lander-scale slope from higher-resolution models, relay satellites and side-by-side comparison of scenarios.

Vesper is built with Python (NumPy, rasterio, pyproj, requests) for the data pipeline and the offline HTTP server, and with TypeScript, React, Vite and three.js for the web app, tested end to end with Playwright, with a voice assistant on the browser's Web Speech API and hosting on GitHub Pages.
